In mathematics, the '''Hurwitz problem''' (named after [[Adolf Hurwitz]]) is the problem of finding multiplicative relations between [[quadratic form]]s which generalise those known to exist between sums of squares in certain numbers of variables.

==Description==
There are well-known multiplicative relationships between sums of squares in two variables

:<math> (x^2+y^2)(u^2+v^2) = (xu-yv)^2 + (xv+yu)^2 \ , </math>

(known as the [[Brahmagupta–Fibonacci identity]]), and also [[Euler's four-square identity]] and [[Degen's eight-square identity]]. These may be interpreted as multiplicativity for the norms on the [[complex number]]s (<math>\mathbb{C}</math>), [[quaternion]]s (<math>\mathbb{H}</math>), and [[octonion]]s (<math>\mathbb{O}</math>), respectively.<ref name=Rajwade>{{cite book | first=A.R. | last=Rajwade | year=1993 | title=Squares | series=London Mathematical Society Lecture Note Series | volume=171 | publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] | isbn=0-521-42668-5 | zbl=0785.11022 }}</ref>{{rp|1–3}}<ref>{{cite book |first=C.W. |last=Curtis |author-link=Charles W. Curtis |year=1963 |section=The four and eight square problem and division algebras |title=Studies in Modern Algebra |editor=Albert, A.A. |pages=100–125, esp. 115 |publisher=[[Mathematical Association of America]]}} — Solution of Hurwitz's Problem on page 115.</ref>

The Hurwitz problem for the field {{mvar|K}} is to find general relations of the form

:<math> (x_1^2+\cdots+x_r^2) \cdot (y_1^2+\cdots+y_s^2) = (z_1^2 + \cdots + z_n^2) \ , </math>

with the {{mvar|z}} being bilinear forms in the {{mvar|x}} and {{mvar|y}}: that is, each {{mvar|z}} is a {{mvar|K}}-linear combination of terms of the form {{mvar|x{{sub|i}} y{{sub|j}}}}.<ref name=Lam>{{cite book | first=Tsit-Yuen | last=Lam | author-link=Tsit Yuen Lam | year=2005 | title=Introduction to Quadratic Forms over Fields | series=[[Graduate Studies in Mathematics]] | volume=67 | publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] | isbn=0-8218-1095-2 | zbl=1068.11023 | mr = 2104929 }}</ref>{{rp|127}}

We call a triple <math>\; (r, s, n) \;</math> ''admissible'' for {{mvar|K}} if such an identity exists.<ref name=Rajwade/>{{rp|125}} Trivial cases of admissible triples include <math>\; (r, s, rs) \;.</math> The problem is uninteresting for {{mvar|K}} of [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]]&nbsp;2, since over such fields every sum of squares is a square, and we exclude this case. It is believed that otherwise admissibility is independent of the field of definition.<ref name=Rajwade/>{{rp|137}}

== The Hurwitz–Radon theorem ==
Hurwitz posed the problem in 1898 in the special case <math>\; r = s = n \;</math> and showed that, when coefficients are taken in <math>\mathbb{C}</math>, the only admissible values <math>\, (n, n, n) \,</math> were <math>\; n \in \{ 1, 2, 4, 8 \} \;.</math><ref name=Lam/>{{rp|130}} His proof extends to a field of any [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] ''except''&nbsp;2.<ref name=Rajwade/>{{rp|3}}

The "Hurwitz–Radon" problem is that of finding admissible triples of the form <math>\, (r, n, n) \;.</math> Obviously <math>\; (1, n, n) \;</math> is admissible. The '''Hurwitz–Radon theorem''' states that <math>\; \left( \rho(n), n, n \right) \;</math> is admissible over any field where <math>\, \rho(n) \,</math> is the function defined for <math>\; n = 2^u v\;,</math> {{mvar|v}} odd, <math>\; u = 4 a + b \;,</math> with <math>\; 0 \le b \le 3 \;,</math> and <math>\; \rho(n) = 8 a + 2^b\;.</math><ref name=Rajwade/>{{rp|137}}<ref name=Lam/>{{rp|130}}

Other admissible triples include <math>\, (3, 5, 7) \,</math><ref name=Rajwade/>{{rp|138}} and <math>\, (10, 10, 16) \;.</math><ref name=Rajwade/>{{rp|137}}
